lessonActivities.title: What Are Question Tags? 🎯
lessonActivities.content:
Ever said 'It's nice, isn't it?' or 'You're coming, aren't you?'? 🙋 Those are question tags! They turn statements into mini-questions to seek agreement or confirmation. 📚

Basic Rule: Positive statement → Negative tag | Negative statement → Positive tag

StatementTagExampleFunction
PositiveNegativeShe lives in Tokyo, doesn't she?Seeking agreement
NegativePositiveHe can't drive, can he?Checking confirmation

Fun fact: Question tags are far more common in speaking than writing—they make conversations feel interactive! 💡
examples: Agreement: You've seen this film, haven't you?
Confirmation: The train isn't late, is it?
functions: Identify when to use question tags
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Quick Rule: Same auxiliary in tag as in statement. Flip the sign: + statement → - tag, - statement → + tag.

lessonActivities.title: Forming Tags with Auxiliary Verbs 🚀
lessonActivities.content:
When the statement has an auxiliary verb (be, have, do) or a modal (can, will, should), use that same verb in the tag! 🎮

Pattern: [Statement with auxiliary] + [same auxiliary + not/not + subject pronoun]?

Auxiliary in StatementTag PatternExampleSubject Pronoun
is/are/was/wereisn't/aren't/wasn't/weren't + pronounHe is tall, isn't he?he/she/it/they
have/has/hadhaven't/hasn't/hadn't + pronounThey've left, haven't they?they/we/you
can/could/will/wouldcan't/couldn't/won't/wouldn't + pronounYou can swim, can't you?you/I/we

Fun fact: The subject in the tag is ALWAYS a pronoun, never a name or noun! ✅ 'John is here, isn't he?' NOT 'isn't John?' 🌟
examples: Be-verb: The bus stop's over there, isn't it?
Modal: They could hear me, couldn't they?
Perfect: Your parents have retired, haven't they?
functions: Match auxiliary verbs to tag forms
Convert nouns to pronouns in tags
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Memory trick: Copy the auxiliary, flip the sign, swap noun for pronoun. Done! ✨

lessonActivities.title: Tags with No Auxiliary: Do/Does/Did 🌟
lessonActivities.content:
What if the statement has NO auxiliary verb? 🤔 For present simple or past simple positive statements, we add do/does/did in the tag!

Pattern: [Subject + main verb] + [do/does/did + not + pronoun]?

Statement TenseTag AuxiliaryExampleWhy?
Present Simpledo/doesJenni eats cheese, doesn't she?No auxiliary in statement
Past SimpledidI said that already, didn't I?Need auxiliary for tag
Verb = be (present/past)am/is/are/was/wereNone were happy, were they?'Be' IS the auxiliary

Fun fact: Even though 'be' is a main verb, it acts like an auxiliary for tags—so no 'do' needed! 🎨
examples: Present: She works hard, doesn't she?
Past: They arrived early, didn't they?
Be-verb exception: You're tired, aren't you? (NOT 'don't you?')
functions: Distinguish 'be' as auxiliary vs. main verb
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Decision point: Does the statement already have am/is/are/was/were/have/can/will? → Use that. No auxiliary? → Add do/does/did.

lessonActivities.title: Special Cases: Aren't I? Shall We? Will You? ⚡
lessonActivities.content:
English loves exceptions! 🤯 Three question tag patterns break the usual rules—let's master them:

StatementStandard Rule Would GiveActual TagReason
I am...amn't I? ❌aren't I? ✅'Amn't' doesn't exist in standard English
Let's...don't we? ❌shall we? ✅'Let's' = 'let us' → suggestion → 'shall' for proposals
Imperative (You...)do you? ❌will you? / won't you? ✅Softens commands into polite requests

Examples:

  • I'm never on time, aren't I? (NOT 'amn't I?')
  • Let's go now, shall we? (Making a suggestion)
  • Close the door, will you? (Polite request)

Fun fact: 'Aren't I?' is one of the most accepted 'irregular' forms in English—even in formal speech! 🎯
examples: I'm clever, aren't I? ✅
Let's leave, shall we? ✅
Pass the salt, will you? ✅ (polite)
functions: Apply exception rules for I am / Let's / imperatives
Choose appropriate tag for politeness level
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Pro tip: Memorize these three: I am → aren't I? | Let's → shall we? | Command → will you?

lessonActivities.title: Negative Meaning Words & Tags 🎯
lessonActivities.content:
Words like never, seldom, rarely, hardly, nobody have negative meaning—even if the verb looks positive! 🎨 This affects your tag choice.

Rule: If the statement contains a negative-meaning word → treat it as NEGATIVE → use POSITIVE tag.

Negative WordStatement ExampleCorrect TagWhy?
neverShe never calls, ___?does she?'Never' = negative meaning
seldomHe seldom travels, ___?does he?'Seldom' = rarely = negative
nobodyNobody called, ___?did they?'Nobody' = not anybody
hardlyThey hardly ever come, ___?do they?'Hardly' = almost never

⚠️ Common mistake: ❌ 'She never calls, doesn't she?' → ✅ 'does she?' (positive tag because 'never' is negative)

Fun fact: These words are called 'negative adverbs' or 'semi-negatives'—they flip the polarity without using 'not'! 🌍
examples: He hardly knows her, does he? ✅
Nothing happened, did it? ✅
Rarely do they complain, do they? ✅
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 When to use: Scan for never/seldom/rarely/hardly/nobody/nothing. If found → positive tag, even if verb looks positive.

lessonActivities.title: Intonation: Falling vs. Rising ❓
lessonActivities.content:
Question tags aren't just about grammar—they're about intonation too! 🎵 How you say the tag changes its meaning.

Falling intonation (↘): You're sure; you expect agreement.
Rising intonation (↗): You're less sure; you're genuinely asking.

IntonationSpeaker CertaintyExample (written)Spoken Meaning
Falling ↘High certaintyIt's cold, isn't it? ↘'I think it's cold; agree with me.'
Rising ↗Low certaintyIt's cold, isn't it? ↗'Is it cold? I'm not sure—tell me.'
Falling ↘Polite assumptionYou're coming, aren't you? ↘'I assume you're coming; confirm please.'

Note: In writing, we can't show intonation—but context clues help! Formal writing often avoids tags; informal writing may add (↘) or (↗) for clarity.

Fun fact: Native speakers use falling intonation for tags about 80% of the time—they're usually seeking agreement, not information! 💬
examples: Agreement-seeking: You like coffee, don't you? ↘
Genuine question: This is the right way, isn't it? ↗
Polite confirmation: We'll meet at 5, won't we? ↘
functions: Choose appropriate tag for intended certainty level
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Remember: In writing, if the statement sounds confident → tag seeks agreement. If uncertain → tag asks for info.

lessonActivities.title: Tags in Reported Speech & Complex Sentences 🕐
lessonActivities.content:
Question tags get tricky in reported speech and complex sentences! ⚠️ The tag always refers to the MAIN clause's subject and auxiliary.

Rule: Ignore subordinate clauses. Find the main subject + auxiliary → form tag from those.

Sentence TypeMain ClauseCorrect TagCommon Error
Reported speechShe said (that) he was latedidn't she?❌ 'wasn't he?' (wrong subject)
Relative clauseThe man who called you is hereisn't he?❌ 'didn't he?' (wrong clause)
ConditionalIf it rains, we'll stay homewon't we?❌ 'doesn't it?' (wrong clause)

⚠️ Common mistake: ❌ 'She said he was late, wasn't he?' → ✅ 'didn't she?' (tag refers to 'She said', not 'he was late')

Fun fact: Even advanced learners mix up tag subjects in complex sentences—focus on the MAIN verb! 🎯
examples: Reported: He told us they'd won, didn't he?
Relative: The book that I borrowed is great, isn't it?
Conditional: If you need help, just ask, will you?
functions: Identify main clause in complex sentences
Form tags based on main subject/auxiliary
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Never forget: Find the MAIN subject + verb FIRST. Ignore 'that...', 'who...', 'if...' clauses when forming tags.

lessonActivities.title: Mastery: Tags for Politeness & Nuance 🏆
lessonActivities.content:
You've mastered the rules—now let's use tags for social nuance! 🌟 Question tags can soften requests, show empathy, or invite collaboration.

Polite Requests: Use 'will you?', 'would you?', 'could you?' after imperatives.
Empathetic Tags: Use falling intonation to show shared experience.
Collaborative Tags: Use 'shall we?' to include the listener in decisions.

Context / PurposeTag ChoiceExampleEffect
Polite commandwill you? / would you?Pass the salt, would you?Softens order → request
Shared experienceisn't it? / don't you? (falling)What a day, isn't it? ↘Builds rapport, invites agreement
Joint decisionshall we?Let's start, shall we?Inclusive, collaborative tone
Checking understandingright? / okay? (informal)We meet at 5, okay?Casual confirmation

Mastery checklist: ✅ Flip polarity correctly ✅ Match auxiliary/modal ✅ Handle special cases (aren't I?, shall we?) ✅ Adjust for negative-meaning words ✅ Choose intonation for intended meaning

Fun fact: In some dialects, invariant tags like 'innit?' (isn't it?) or 'eh?' are used for all statements—standard English prefers precise matching! 🎓
examples: Polite: Open the window, could you?
Empathetic: Tough exam, wasn't it? ↘
Collaborative: Let's review this, shall we?
Casual: You're joining us, right?
functions: Adapt tag choice to formality and relationship
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Master level: In formal contexts, use precise tags. In casual speech, invariant tags ('right?', 'okay?') are acceptable—but know the difference!

quizActivities.question: What tag follows a positive statement?
quizActivities.explanation: Question tags reverse polarity: positive statements take negative tags to seek agreement or confirmation.

quizActivities.question: Which tag is correct for 'I am'?
quizActivities.hint: Special case: 'amn't' doesn't exist in standard English
quizActivities.explanation: 'Aren't I?' is the standard negative tag for 'I am' statements, even though it seems irregular.

quizActivities.question: What tag follows 'Let's'?
quizActivities.explanation: 'Let's' is a contraction of 'let us', used for suggestions. The conventional tag is 'shall we?' to invite agreement.

quizActivities.question: Tag for negative-meaning word:
quizActivities.explanation: Words like seldom, never, hardly have negative meaning even without 'not'. Treat the statement as negative → use positive tag.

quizActivities.question: Tag for imperative:
quizActivities.hint: Imperatives → will you? / won't you? for politeness
quizActivities.explanation: After commands, 'will you?' or 'won't you?' softens the imperative into a polite request. Both are acceptable.

quizActivities.question: Tag for complex sentence:
quizActivities.sentence: She said that he was late, ____?
quizActivities.hint: Tag refers to MAIN clause subject + auxiliary
quizActivities.explanation: In complex sentences, the tag always matches the main clause ('She said'), not subordinate clauses ('that he was late').

quizActivities.question: Intonation for agreement-seeking:
quizActivities.explanation: Falling intonation on the tag signals the speaker is confident and seeks confirmation. Rising intonation signals genuine uncertainty.

quizActivities.question: Tag for 'nobody':
quizActivities.hint: 'Nobody' = negative → positive tag; use 'they' for indefinite subjects
quizActivities.explanation: 'Nobody' has negative meaning, so use positive tag. For indefinite subjects (nobody, somebody), use 'they' in the tag.

quizActivities.question: Formal vs. informal tag:
quizActivities.hint: Formal: precise auxiliary match. Informal: invariant tags
quizActivities.explanation: In formal contexts, use grammatically precise tags matching the auxiliary. Informal speech may use invariant tags like 'right?' or 'okay?'.

quizActivities.question: Tag for modal 'must':
quizActivities.hint: Modal in statement → same modal in tag
quizActivities.explanation: When the statement contains a modal verb (must, can, will), the tag uses the same modal: 'must' → 'mustn't'.

quizActivities.question: Identify the error:
quizActivities.explanation: 'Never' makes the statement negative in meaning, so the tag should be positive: 'does she?', not 'doesn't she?'.

quizActivities.question: Tag for past perfect:
quizActivities.explanation: When the statement uses past perfect ('had left'), the tag uses the same auxiliary 'had': 'hadn't they?'.

quizActivities.question: Advanced: Tag for conditional main clause:
quizActivities.hint: Tag matches MAIN clause: 'we'll cancel' → won't we?
quizActivities.explanation: Even in conditional sentences, the tag refers to the main clause ('we'll cancel'), not the if-clause ('If it rains').

quizActivities.question: Tag for emphatic 'do':
quizActivities.hint: Emphatic 'do' still counts as auxiliary → don't you?
quizActivities.explanation: Even when 'do' is used for emphasis ('You DO like...'), it functions as the auxiliary for tag formation: 'don't you?'.

quizActivities.question: Most natural informal tag:
quizActivities.hint: Informal speech allows invariant tags like 'right?' or 'okay?'
quizActivities.explanation: In casual conversation, invariant tags ('right?', 'okay?', 'innit?') are common and natural, though precise tags ('wasn't it?') are always correct.
